name: Historical materialism
summary: Historical materialism is the Marx–Engels theory that how people produce their means of life (productive forces and relations of production) forms the economic base that conditions law, politics and ideas. Societies move through successive modes of production, driven by struggle between classes whose interests are irreconcilable where one class lives off another's labour. The state is read as an instrument of the ruling class and religion and the ruling ideas as reflections of social being. Capitalism is credited with a revolutionary role in developing production, and the sources look to its replacement by social ownership, planned production, a transitional proletarian state and finally a communist society where the state dies out and goods go by need.
scope: Historical materialism as the theory of history and society that Marx and Engels set out in The German Ideology and the 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy: the way people produce their means of life (the productive forces and the relations of production) forms the economic base, which conditions the legal, political and ideological superstructure; societies pass through successive modes of production driven by class struggle, and capitalism gives way to communism. The sources name Engels as the coiner of the term (Blackledge, s2), Plekhanov and Kautsky as the generation that systematised it (Rigby, s1), the Soviet textbooks (Glezerman and Kursanov, Berbeshkina, Boguslavsky, s4, s5, s8) and Bukharin (s6) as its codified form, and G. A. Cohen's reconstruction as its analytic landmark (Rigby, Anderson, s1, s3). It is the theory of history, not the whole of Marxism: Marx's economics and the strategy of the parties that used it are excluded unless the sources present them as part of this theory. Dialectical materialism, which the Soviet textbooks treat as its inseparable philosophical companion (s4), is in scope only where those textbooks join the two. Later Marxisms that reject its determinism (Rigby's critique, s1) are not the subject but are critics' views of it.
